![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212968/assets/d2e2666baf2931dc4e0d8ba097a364b7b7a1bba75e65c8d802a60180e9a94854.png)

Neah is flying a kite $K$ with a string of length $112\,\text{ft}.$ The angle of elevation $\theta $ of the kite is increasing at a rate of $\frac{\pi }{28}$ radians per second. Find, as a function of $\theta ,$ the rate at which the kite's altitude is increasing.
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212968/assets/8c3c9e40f56d0b269562c37fd2d87c7e8f0394c8f55dca596e5e751f5e96157b.png)

  

In the figure, $y$ is the altitude of the kite, and $z$ is the distance between the kite and Neah. The quantity $z=112\,\text{ft}$ does not change with time because the kite string's length is fixed.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}.$
To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $y$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $y$ and $z$ are the opposite and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{z} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{112} \\ y & =112\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(112\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =(112\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=\frac{\pi }{28}.$ Substituting these values into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =(112\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\frac{\pi }{28} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =4\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate at which the kite is gaining altitude is $4\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\,\text{ft/s}.$
